lessons.title: Collections and LINQ
lessons.explanation:
# 03 · Collections and LINQ

This is the module you will use every day. Nearly all business code is
"take these records, keep some, reshape them, group them, add them up" —
and in .NET that means picking a container and writing a query.

Two skills, and they fail in different ways. Choosing the wrong container
makes correct code slow. Misunderstanding LINQ's laziness makes fast code
wrong.

## The mental model

### 1 · Three containers cover almost everything

| container | good at | bad at | order |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `List<T>` | indexing, appending, iterating | `Contains` (O(n)) | insertion |
| `Dictionary<K,V>` | key lookup (O(1)) | anything ordered | **none** |
| `HashSet<T>` | membership, dedupe (O(1)) | indexing | **none** |

`Dictionary` and `HashSet` need a sane `GetHashCode` on the key. Records,
value tuples, strings and primitives have one. A plain `class` does not —
it hashes by reference, so two "equal" keys are two entries.

`HashSet<T>.Add` returns `false` when the item was already there. That one
return value collapses "have I seen this?" and "remember it" into a single
probe, and it is the backbone of every dedupe you will write.

### 2 · A query is a recipe, not a result

```csharp
var q = items.Where(Expensive);   // nothing has run
var a = q.ToList();               // NOW it runs
var b = q.ToList();               // and it runs AGAIN
```

Deferred execution buys you two things — early exit (`First` over a
million rows stops at the first hit) and composition — and costs you two:
the query re-runs on every enumeration, and it reads whatever the source
holds *at that moment*, not when you wrote it.

The rule that follows: **materialise before you cross a boundary.** A
method that returns `List<T>` returns a value; one that returns a lazy
`IEnumerable<T>` returns a promise the caller can accidentally cash twice.

### 3 · Pick the operator whose shape matches the question

```csharp
customers.Join(orders, ...)       // one row per MATCHING PAIR   (inner join)
customers.GroupJoin(orders, ...)  // one row per LEFT ITEM       (left join)
sales.GroupBy(s => s.Region)      // one group per distinct key
```

If the answer must have one row per customer, `Join` is already wrong: a
customer with three orders appears three times and every total is
multiplied. That is fan-out, and it is the same bug in SQL.

### 4 · Every fold is three decisions

What the accumulator holds, what the seed is, and how one item updates it.
Choose the seed so the empty case falls out for free.

```csharp
results.Aggregate((Wins: 0, Losses: 0), (t, r) => r == "w" ? (t.Wins + 1, t.Losses) : (t.Wins, t.Losses + 1));
```

## The details that bite

1. **`Average`, `Max`, `Min`, `First`, `Single` and seedless `Aggregate`
   throw on an empty sequence.** "Sequence contains no elements" never
   tells you which query. Decide what empty means and say it.
2. **Multiple enumeration.** `source.Max() - source.Min()` walks the
   sequence twice. On a `List` that is waste; on a generator, a file, or
   a database query it is a bug. In review: an `IEnumerable<T>` parameter
   used twice in one method.
3. **`OrderBy` twice is not a tie-breaker.** The second call re-sorts from
   scratch. Use `ThenBy`.
4. **Sorting numeric strings sorts them as text** — `"10"` before `"9"`.
   Project to a number in the key selector.
5. **The `Dictionary` indexer throws on read and creates on write.**
   `TryGetValue` answers both questions in one hash probe;
   `ContainsKey` + indexer hashes twice and races.
6. **`Distinct` and `GroupBy` use the default equality comparer.** For a
   class that means reference equality, so "duplicates" survive. Use a
   record, a key selector (`DistinctBy`), or a comparer.
7. **`GroupBy` buffers.** It cannot yield a group before reading the whole
   source, so it is deferred but not streaming.
8. **`List.Sort` is unstable, LINQ's `OrderBy` is stable.** If equal items
   must keep their input order, that difference is your answer.
9. **A `HashSet` has no order.** It will look insertion-ordered in a small
   test and stop being so after a removal.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-pick-the-collection.cs` | ★☆☆ | dedupe, tally and duplicate-detect — with the right container |
| 02 | `02-dictionary-patterns.cs` | ★☆☆ | the four ways to read a dictionary, and a hand-built index |
| 03 | `03-select-where-flatten.cs` | ★☆☆ | `Where` / `Select` / `SelectMany`, and the empty-sequence crash |
| 04 | `04-grouping.cs` | ★★☆ | group-then-aggregate: totals, best sellers, group sizes |
| 05 | `05-joins.cs` | ★★☆ | inner join vs left join, and the row that quietly disappears |
| 06 | `06-ordering.cs` | ★★☆ | primary + tie-breaker, descending, and "10" before "9" |
| 07 | `07-aggregate-and-fold.cs` | ★★☆ | running totals, a two-number accumulator, a longest streak |
| 08 | `08-deferred-execution.cs` | ★★★ | one query that must be eager, one that must be lazy, one that must read once |

Do them in order — 08 is where the first seven turn into a mental model,
and it is the file that will change how you write method signatures.

```
dotnet run exercises/04-grouping.cs
dotnet run solutions/04-grouping.cs
dotnet run ../verify.cs 03
dotnet run ../progress.cs 03
```

---

**Stuck?** `cheatsheets/linq.md` (every operator, what it costs, what it throws) · **Self-check:** `quizzes/03-collections-and-linq.md` · **Next:** `bootcamp/04-strings-and-time`

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/01-pi.instructions:
**Concepts:** List · Dictionary · HashSet · lookup cost  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Three jobs. Each one is easy with the right container and quadratic
with the wrong one.

    Unique(["a","b","a"])       → ["a", "b"]   (first-seen order kept)
    Counts(["a","b","a"])       → { a: 2, b: 1 }
    AnyDuplicates([1, 2, 1])    → true

Unique must keep the order the items first appeared in — the naive
"sort and dedupe" answer is wrong here.

hint: HashSet<T>.Add returns FALSE when the item was already there,
which answers "have I seen this?" and records it in one step and one
hash lookup. Dictionary has CollectionsMarshal-free helpers too:
TryGetValue, GetValueOrDefault, and an indexer that creates on write.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/01-pi.explanation:
All three answers are the same answer: a hash-based container turns
"have I seen this?" from a scan into a single probe. The version
everyone writes first — `if (!result.Contains(tag))` on a List — is
O(n) per item and O(n squared) overall, which is invisible on the
three-item test and painful on the fifty-thousand-row import.
HashSet.Add doing double duty (adding AND telling you whether it was
new) is the trick worth memorising: it collapses check-then-act into
one operation, which also removes the race in concurrent code.
Unique keeps insertion order because it iterates the source and uses
the set only as a filter. A HashSet itself has NO defined order —
never enumerate one and rely on what comes out. Distinct() from LINQ
does exactly this and is what you would ship; writing it once by hand
is how you know what it costs.
Counts uses GetValueOrDefault so the first sighting starts from zero
without a Contains check. The Dictionary indexer creates on write and
throws on read of a missing key — an asymmetry that surprises people
exactly once.
Cost table worth carrying: List indexing O(1), List.Contains O(n),
Dictionary and HashSet lookup O(1) average, and both of those need a
sane GetHashCode on the key type — which you get free from records
and value tuples, and must write by hand for a class.

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/02-di.instructions:
**Concepts:** TryGetValue · GetValueOrDefault · building an index  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A Dictionary read has four spellings and they behave differently on
a missing key. This exercise makes you use the right one three
times.

    Lookup(map, "missing")           → ""      (never throws)
    IndexByFirstLetter(["ant","bee","ape"])
                                     → { a: ["ant","ape"], b: ["bee"] }
    Invert({ a: "1", b: "2" })       → { 1: "a", 2: "b" }

Invert on duplicate values keeps the LAST one seen — say so in the
code rather than letting an exception decide.

hint: the indexer THROWS on a missing read and CREATES on a write.
TryGetValue answers both questions in one probe.
CollectionsMarshal aside, `if (!map.TryGetValue(k, out var list)) {
list = new(); map[k] = list; }` is the standard grouping shape.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/02-di.explanation:
The four reads, and when each is right:
  map[key]                  throws if missing — use when absence is a bug
  map.TryGetValue(k, out v) one probe, tells you and gives you the value
  map.GetValueOrDefault(k)  one probe, absence becomes default(T)
  map.ContainsKey(k)        a probe that answers only half the question
`if (map.ContainsKey(k)) use(map[k]);` hashes the key TWICE and, in
concurrent code, can be wrong between the two lines. TryGetValue is
the same code with one lookup and no race.
IndexByFirstLetter is the manual GroupBy, and the shape — try to get
the bucket, create it if it is not there, then add — is the same
shape you will write for caches, adjacency lists and multi-maps.
Note the assignment `map[key] = list` after creating: the indexer
CREATES on write, which is the asymmetry with the throwing read.
Invert says out loud that the last duplicate wins. The alternative,
ToDictionary(v => v.Value, v => v.Key), throws ArgumentException on a
duplicate — fine when duplicates are impossible, a production
incident when they are merely unlikely. Deciding explicitly is the
lesson; the exception is not a decision.
A dictionary has no order. It looks insertion-ordered in small tests
and stops being so after a removal — never rely on it.

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/03-se.instructions:
**Concepts:** Where · Select · SelectMany · empty sequences  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

The three verbs that do most of the work in any codebase. A User
record is defined at the BOTTOM of this file.

    ActiveNames(users)        → the names of the active ones, in order
    Flatten([["a"],["b","c"]])→ ["a", "b", "c"]
    AverageAge(users)         → 0 for an empty list, NOT an exception

That last one is the whole point of the exercise: LINQ's Average
THROWS on an empty sequence, and nearly every "sequence contains no
elements" crash in production is this line.

hint: Select maps one to one, SelectMany maps one to many and
concatenates. For the average, ask whether there is anything to
average before averaging — Any() is the cheap question.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/03-se.explanation:
Where filters and keeps order. Select maps one element to one
element. SelectMany maps one element to a SEQUENCE and concatenates
the results, which is why it handles the empty group for free — an
empty inner sequence contributes nothing rather than a null hole.
These are the three shapes almost every data transformation reduces
to, and reading a pipeline as filter-project-flatten is how you make
sense of somebody else's forty-line query.
AverageAge is the real lesson. Average, Max, Min, First, Last, Single
and Aggregate-without-a-seed all THROW on an empty sequence, and the
message ("Sequence contains no elements") never says which query. The
fix is to decide what empty MEANS: here it is 0, elsewhere it might
be null or a sentinel, but it is a product decision either way. The
alternatives worth knowing: DefaultIfEmpty(0), or Average over a
nullable projection which returns null instead of throwing.
Note the tests call ToList inside the helpers rather than returning a
lazy query. Returning List<T> from a method whose name sounds like a
noun ("ActiveNames") is honest: the caller gets a value, not a
promise that will re-run when they enumerate it twice.

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/04-gr.instructions:
**Concepts:** GroupBy · ToLookup · aggregating a group  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Sale records are defined at the BOTTOM of this file. Three reports:

    TotalByRegion(sales)   → { "north": 300m, "south": 150m }
    BestSellerPerRegion(s) → { "north": "widget", ... }  (highest total)
    RegionsWithAtLeast(s, 2)
                           → regions with 2 or more sales, sorted A-Z

Every region that appears in the data appears in the first two
reports, and no region that does not.

hint: GroupBy(keySelector) gives you a sequence of groups; each
group IS an IEnumerable of its items and also carries a .Key. You
can go straight to a dictionary with ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g =>
...). MaxBy on a group answers "which item is biggest".
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/04-gr.explanation:
GroupBy turns a flat sequence into a sequence of groups, where each
group is itself enumerable and carries a Key. Almost every report you
will ever write is group-then-aggregate, and the only variation is
what the aggregate is: Sum, Count, MaxBy, or another GroupBy.
BestSellerPerRegion is the two-level version and the one people get
wrong: you must aggregate WITHIN each region before comparing, or you
pick the single biggest line item rather than the biggest product.
The "sums a product before comparing" test is there precisely to
catch the naive MaxBy(s => s.Amount).
MaxBy (and MinBy) return the ELEMENT, not the value — the LINQ method
people reimplement by hand for years before noticing it exists. On an
empty sequence they return null rather than throwing, unlike Max.
GroupBy is deferred but it BUFFERS: it must read the whole source
before it can yield the first group, because it cannot know a group
is complete until the input ends. If you only need lookups and not a
report, ToLookup does the same work eagerly and, unlike a Dictionary,
returns an empty sequence for a missing key instead of throwing.
Ordering: GroupBy preserves the order in which keys first appear, and
the order of items inside each group. That is guaranteed for LINQ to
Objects and NOT for a database provider — never lean on it in EF.

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/05-jo.instructions:
**Concepts:** Join · GroupJoin · left join · DefaultIfEmpty  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Customers and Orders (records at the BOTTOM of this file). Three
questions, and the difference between them is the whole lesson:

    NamesWithOrders(c, o)      → names that have at least one order
    TotalPerCustomer(c, o)     → EVERY customer, with 0 for no orders
    CustomersWithoutOrders(c,o)→ the names with nothing

TotalPerCustomer is a LEFT join: a customer who never bought
anything still appears, with a total of zero. Getting that wrong —
silently dropping the rows with nothing to show — is one of the most
common reporting bugs there is, because the report still looks
plausible.

hint: Join gives you inner-join pairs. GroupJoin gives you each left
item together with its (possibly empty) group of matches, which is
exactly what a left join is. Sort the outputs A-Z.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/05-jo.explanation:
Join is an INNER join: it emits one result per matching PAIR, so a
customer with two orders appears twice. That is why NamesWithOrders
needs Distinct — and why a naive Join used for a total double-counts.
The row multiplication is called fan-out, and it is the reason a
report can be exactly right on customers with one order and wrong on
everybody else.
GroupJoin is the left join: for each left item you get the item plus
a group of its matches, and the group is EMPTY rather than absent
when nothing matched. Sum over an empty sequence is 0, so the "no
orders" case needs no special handling at all — the shape of the
operator gives you the right answer.
That is the general lesson: pick the operator whose SHAPE matches the
question. If the answer must have one row per left item, you want
GroupJoin. If it must have one row per pair, you want Join. Deciding
that first prevents both the dropped-rows bug and the double-counting
bug, and it maps one-to-one onto SQL's INNER and LEFT JOIN.
DefaultIfEmpty is the other spelling: GroupJoin followed by
SelectMany with DefaultIfEmpty flattens back to pairs with nulls,
which is exactly what SQL's LEFT JOIN emits.
Performance: Join and GroupJoin build a hash lookup over the inner
sequence, so they are O(n + m), not the O(n * m) you get from a
nested Where. That is a real reason to use them over a loop.

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/06-or.instructions:
**Concepts:** OrderBy · ThenBy · stability · comparing strings as numbers  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A Ticket record is defined at the BOTTOM of this file.

    ByLengthThenAlpha(["bb","a","cc"])  → ["a", "bb", "cc"]
    TopPriority(tickets, 2)             → the two most urgent,
                                          ties broken by title A-Z
    SortNumeric(["10","9","2"])         → ["2", "9", "10"]

SortNumeric receives strings that hold numbers. Sorting them as text
puts "10" before "9", which is correct for text and wrong for the
answer anybody wanted.

hint: OrderBy then ThenBy expresses "primary, then tie-breaker" —
calling OrderBy twice throws the first sort away. Descending has its
own method. LINQ's OrderBy is STABLE (equal items keep their input
order); List.Sort is not.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/06-or.explanation:
OrderBy starts a sort; ThenBy adds a tie-breaker to the SAME sort.
Writing OrderBy twice does not layer them — the second one re-sorts
from scratch and the first is wasted work with a misleading name.
That is the single most common LINQ ordering bug, and it is invisible
until two items tie.
TopPriority combines descending primary with ascending secondary,
which reads exactly as the requirement does: most urgent first, ties
alphabetical. Take after ordering is fine — LINQ to Objects will
still sort the whole sequence, but the intent is clear and the cost
only matters at scale (where you would reach for a heap; see the
data-structures module).
SortNumeric is the "10 before 9" trap. Sorting text compares
character by character, so "10" < "9" because '1' < '9'. Projecting
to a number in the key selector fixes it while KEEPING the original
strings in the output — that is why the key selector exists rather
than transforming the sequence first. The "007" test proves you did
not accidentally return the parsed numbers.
Stability: LINQ's OrderBy is documented stable, so equal keys stay in
input order — worth relying on. List.Sort and Array.Sort use an
unstable introsort, so equal elements can be reordered. If ties must
keep their order, either use LINQ or add an explicit tie-breaker.
For a custom rule you cannot express as a key, OrderBy has an
overload taking an IComparer<T>. Reach for the key selector first —
a comparer that is not a total order (inconsistent ties) will throw
"IComparer.Compare() method returns inconsistent results".

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/07-ag.instructions:
**Concepts:** Aggregate · accumulators · seeds  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Sum and Count are folds with the boring accumulator. Here are three
with interesting ones:

    RunningTotals([1,2,3])        → [1, 3, 6]
    Tally(["w","l","w"])          → (Wins: 2, Losses: 1)
    LongestStreak(["w","w","l","w"]) → 2

A streak is the longest run of consecutive "w". Every one of these
must work on an empty sequence without special-casing it at the top
— pick a seed that makes the empty case fall out.

hint: Aggregate(seed, (accumulator, item) => nextAccumulator). The
accumulator can be a tuple when you need to carry two numbers, which
is exactly what a streak needs: the best so far and the current run.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/07-ag.explanation:
Every fold is the same three decisions: what the accumulator holds,
what the seed is, and how one item updates it. Get those right and
the code writes itself; get the SEED right and the empty case
disappears without an if.
Tally carries two numbers, so the accumulator is a tuple seeded with
(0, 0). LongestStreak carries two as well — the best run seen and the
run in progress — because you cannot know the best without tracking
the current, and you cannot track the current without resetting it.
Seeding with (0, 0) is what makes both the empty sequence and the
all-losses case answer 0 for free.
The streak fold ends with Math.Max over the pair, which is the part
people forget: the last run has no loss after it to trigger the
comparison, so a sequence ending in wins reports the previous best.
That is the bug the "run that ends the sequence" test exists to
catch, and it is the same off-by-one shape as forgetting to flush a
buffer at end of file.
RunningTotals is a SCAN rather than a fold — it emits an answer per
item instead of one at the end. LINQ has no Scan, so the explicit
loop is the honest version; Aggregate with a list accumulator works
but allocates and reads worse. Knowing when NOT to use Aggregate is
part of using it well: if a plain foreach is clearer, write the
foreach.
One warning: Aggregate with no seed uses the first element as the
seed and THROWS on an empty sequence. Always pass a seed unless you
have already proved the sequence is non-empty.

csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/08-de.instructions:
**Concepts:** deferred execution · multiple enumeration · materialising  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A LINQ query is a RECIPE, not a result. It runs when somebody
enumerates it — every time somebody enumerates it. Three methods
that each depend on getting that right:

    EvensSnapshot(list)   → the evens AS THEY ARE NOW; later edits
                            to the caller's list must not show up
    FirstOver(source, n)  → the first item above n, and it must stop
                            there (the test passes an INFINITE
                            sequence, so eager code hangs forever)
    Distance(source)      → Max - Min, reading the source ONCE
                            (the test counts how often it is walked)

Two of these need you to materialise, one needs you not to, and one
needs you to walk the sequence exactly once. Read the tests.

hint: ToList runs the query and gives you a value. Anything that
returns IEnumerable stays lazy. Two LINQ calls over the same source
walk it twice.
csbootcamp/03-collections-and-linq/08-de.explanation:
Where, Select, OrderBy and friends return a query OBJECT. Nothing has
happened yet. The work starts when something enumerates it — foreach,
ToList, Count, First — and it starts AGAIN on the next enumeration.
EvensSnapshot: returning `source.Where(...)` compiles and passes the
first test, then fails the second, because the query still points at
the caller's list and re-reads it when the test enumerates. ToList
turns the recipe into a result. The rule: never hand a lazy query
across a boundary the caller does not control — this is the same bug
as returning a query after the database context is disposed.
FirstOver must stay lazy. FirstOrDefault stops at the first match,
so it terminates on an infinite sequence; `source.Where(...).ToList()
.FirstOrDefault()` would hang forever. Laziness is not just an
optimisation here, it is the difference between working and not.
Distance is the multiple-enumeration trap. `source.Max() -
source.Min()` walks the sequence TWICE, which is invisible on a List
and expensive on a database query, a file read, or a generator — and
simply WRONG on a sequence that cannot be replayed. Materialise once,
then ask both questions.
How to spot it in review: a parameter typed IEnumerable<T> used more
than once in a method body. Either materialise at the top or accept
IReadOnlyList<T> and make the requirement part of the signature.
